headline: 44% of Bangladeshi graduates work informal jobs, World Bank says
summary: A new report highlights a severe shortage of formal employment, with 84% of the total working-age population employed informally.
details: A World Bank study reveals that approximately 44% of university graduates in Bangladesh are working in the informal sector. This trend underscores a critical shortage of formal jobs despite a large working-age population.

The report, titled "Demographic Change in South Asia: From Tailwinds to Headwinds for Development," states that around 84% of the working-age population, or 58 million people, are employed informally.

Informal workers typically lack appointment letters, job security, legal protection, and a standard wage structure. Even in medium and large enterprises, 35% to 40% of workers are employed informally.
Formal businesses in Bangladesh create jobs at an annual rate of just 2.7%, which is significantly lower than the average of 5.4% across 82 emerging economies.

The shortage of regular jobs has pushed many into small businesses. Between 45% and 70% of informal entrepreneurs in Bangladesh, India, and Nepal started their businesses because they could not find other employment.

The World Bank's division director for Bangladesh and Bhutan, Jean Pesme, urged the government to act now to turn the demographic advantage into economic growth by improving skills and removing barriers to women's employment.

The report also highlights critical gaps in healthcare and education. While 70% of the population lives in rural areas, only 20% of healthcare workers are based there, and pre-primary school enrolment is the lowest in South Asia at 36%.
caption:
Nearly half of university graduates in Bangladesh are stuck in informal jobs. Why is the formal job market failing?

A World Bank study reveals that approximately 44% of university graduates in Bangladesh are working in the informal sector. This trend underscores a critical shortage of formal jobs despite a large working-age population.

The report, titled "Demographic Change in South Asia: From Tailwinds to Headwinds for Development," states that around 84% of the working-age population, or 58 million people, are employed informally.

Informal workers typically lack appointment letters, job security, legal protection, and a standard wage structure. Even in medium and large enterprises, 35% to 40% of workers are employed informally.

Formal businesses in Bangladesh create jobs at an annual rate of just 2.7%, which is significantly lower than the average of 5.4% across 82 emerging economies.

The shortage of regular jobs has pushed many into small businesses. Between 45% and 70% of informal entrepreneurs in Bangladesh, India, and Nepal started their businesses because they could not find other employment.

The World Bank's division director for Bangladesh and Bhutan, Jean Pesme, urged the government to act now to turn the demographic advantage into economic growth by improving skills and removing barriers to women's employment.

The report also highlights critical gaps in healthcare and education. While 70% of the population lives in rural areas, only 20% of healthcare workers are based there, and pre-primary school enrolment is the lowest in South Asia at 36%.

headline: Tahsif Souri murder: Friend Ahmed Shahriar Reza Dip gets 3-day remand
summary: Ahmed Shahriar Reza Dip, a friend of the deceased, has been placed on a fresh three-day remand for his alleged involvement in the murder of former Air Force officer KM Tahsif Souri.
details: A Dhaka court has extended the remand of Ahmed Shahriar Reza Dip, a friend of the murdered KM Tahsif Souri, by three days. Dip, 23, is being questioned in connection with the death of Souri, a former Bangladesh Air Force officer.

Police allege that Dip called Souri out of his home on the evening of October 27, and they visited several places together, along with Souri's friend Jarika Tasnim Disha. Disha reportedly left them later that night. Souri's body was recovered from the Turag River the following afternoon.

Investigators stated that Dip and Souri were seen together near the Turag River in Tongi Mazar Bosti around 12:40 am on October 28. Dip reportedly told investigators that they separated after seeing other people in the area. He has provided some information but has also avoided answering certain questions.

The police forwarding report submitted to the court indicates that Dip and Disha were the last people seen with Souri. Investigators believe they have gathered sufficient evidence to suggest their involvement in the murder. Disha, 19, was previously placed on a four-day remand.

Tahsif Souri's father filed a murder case against unidentified individuals on October 31, alleging that his son was killed and his body dumped in the river to conceal the crime. Souri had left his Uttara home on his motorcycle on October 27 and was reported missing before his body was found.
